meta.name: GCP Professional Cloud Network Engineer
meta.notes: Initial pack — 10 questions across PCNE exam domains | 2026-05-23 keyword-balance pass | 2026-06-01 +6 questions to unlock learning path

questions.question: A company has 12 GCP projects organized by team. The platform team owns network resources and must centrally manage firewall rules, subnets, and routes while letting application teams deploy compute in their own projects. Which network architecture meets these requirements?
options: VPC Network Peering links between every application project VPC and a central networking project — VPC peering does not support transitive routing; each application project must peer directly with every other project it needs to reach, and shared services cannot be accessed through a hub via peering
Shared VPC with the platform team's project as the host and application projects as service projects

HA VPN tunnels from each application's VPC to a transit VPC managed by the platform team — application projects each need a separate VPN tunnel to reach shared services, and transitive routing between application projects is not supported natively through VPN
Network Connectivity Center hub with each application project's VPC attached as a spoke
questions.explanation: Shared VPC lets one host project own VPC resources (subnets, firewalls, routes) while service projects deploy workloads into that VPC. Network admins enforce policy centrally without per-project duplication. VPC Peering is non-transitive and does not centralize firewall management. VPNs add tunnel overhead and are intended for hybrid connectivity. NCC connects separate VPCs, but each spoke still owns its own firewalls.

questions.question: An e-commerce site runs identical backend services in us-central1 and europe-west1. Users worldwide must reach the closest healthy region over HTTPS, with TLS terminated as close to them as possible. Which load balancer should you use?
options: Two regional external Application Load Balancers fronted by a Cloud DNS geolocation routing policy with one backend per regional load balancer — dual regional ALBs with DNS geolocation routing require two separate external IPs and do not provide a single anycast IP with automatic cross-region failover
Global external proxy Network Load Balancer with weighted DNS records assigning users to each region
Global external Application Load Balancer with one backend service containing the two regional NEGs
Global external passthrough Network Load Balancer using an anycast IP and regional managed instance groups
questions.explanation: The Global external Application Load Balancer uses an anycast IP, terminates TLS at Google's edge POPs closest to the user, then routes over Google's private backbone to the closest healthy backend region. Regional ALBs with DNS routing suffer from DNS cache TTLs and have no real health-based failover. Passthrough NLBs operate at L4 and cannot terminate TLS. The proxy NLB is also L4 and lacks HTTP-aware routing.

questions.question: You are sizing subnet ranges for a VPC-native GKE cluster expected to grow to 200 nodes with up to 110 pods per node and around 80 ClusterIP Services. Which combination of node subnet primary range plus secondary ranges for pods and services is appropriate?
options: Primary /28 for nodes, secondary /20 for pods, secondary /22 for services
Primary /16 for nodes, secondary /12 for pods, secondary /18 for services
Primary /22 for nodes, secondary /16 for pods, secondary /24 for services
Primary /24 for nodes, secondary /14 for pods, secondary /20 for services
questions.explanation: /22 provides 1024 node addresses, comfortable for 200 nodes plus headroom. The pod range needs roughly nodes × max-pods × 2 for IP allocation slack, so 200 × 110 × 2 ≈ 44,000 — /16 (65,536) fits. /24 accommodates ~80 Services easily. /28 is far too small for 200 nodes. /12 wastes address space and typically exceeds an organization's RFC1918 allocation, increasing peering and on-prem conflicts.

questions.question: All internet egress from a VPC's two regions must flow through a centralized next-hop firewall VM running in us-east1. The default internet route should be overridden for every subnet in the VPC. What is the simplest correct configuration?
options: Add a 0.0.0.0/0 custom static route to the VPC with the firewall VM as the next hop instance, at a priority higher than the default internet route

Run the firewall VM behind Cloud NAT and configure the VPC's default route to use the NAT gateway as the internet next hop — Cloud NAT provides outbound-only NAT for instances without public IPs; it does not allow the firewall VM to function as an internet next hop for other instances' traffic
Enable a Cloud Router with custom advertised routes that send 0.0.0.0/0 toward the firewall VM's internal IP address from its BGP peers
Use VPC Network Peering between two VPCs and apply route export policies that redirect egress traffic through the firewall project
questions.explanation: A 0.0.0.0/0 custom static route with the firewall VM as the next hop instance, given a higher priority (lower numeric value) than the default-internet-gateway route, sends all VPC egress through that VM. Custom routes apply VPC-wide, so both regions follow it. Cloud NAT is a managed service and cannot use a custom VM as next hop. Cloud Router advertises routes to BGP peers, not to local instances. Peering route export does not redirect egress through an appliance.

questions.question: A backend service on GKE in us-central1 must be reachable from on-premises clients over Cloud Interconnect using a single IP, with HTTP path-based routing splitting traffic across multiple Services. Which load balancer is the right fit?
options: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer with multiple frontend ports mapped to backend pods
Internal proxy Network Load Balancer with TCP frontends and host-based routing across backends
Regional internal Application Load Balancer with a URL map and zonal network endpoint groups
Cross-region internal Application Load Balancer with global anycast access from on-premises
questions.explanation: A regional internal Application Load Balancer supports URL maps for HTTP path-based routing and, with global access enabled, is reachable from on-premises networks over Interconnect or HA VPN. Internal passthrough NLB is Layer 4 and cannot route by HTTP path. Internal proxy NLB is also Layer 4 (TCP/TLS), not HTTP-aware. Cross-region internal ALB is multi-region overkill when the backend is single-region.

questions.question: Workloads in a GCP VPC must resolve hostnames in the on-premises corp.example.com Active Directory domain, served by DNS servers reachable over HA VPN. Resolution of other domains should continue to use Cloud DNS and the public internet. What is the correct setup?
options: Create a Cloud DNS private zone for corp.example.com in the VPC and replicate records from on-premises with a scheduled export job
Create a Cloud DNS forwarding zone for corp.example.com with the on-premises DNS server IPs as targets, authorized for the VPC network
Configure an outbound DNS server policy on the VPC pointing to the on-premises DNS servers as alternative name servers for all queries
Set up Cloud DNS peering between the VPC and the on-premises network so Active Directory records are imported into Cloud DNS
questions.explanation: A Cloud DNS forwarding zone sends queries for a specific domain to listed external DNS server IPs reachable over VPN or Interconnect, while other lookups continue through Cloud DNS. Replicating AD records into a private zone is brittle and racy. An outbound server policy forwards ALL queries — including public ones — to the alternative servers. Cloud DNS peering is between two Cloud DNS managed zones in different VPCs, not to on-premises DNS servers.

questions.question: A company needs 12 Gbps of dedicated, low-latency connectivity between a single colocation facility and a GCP VPC with a 99.99% SLA. Which configuration meets the requirement at the lowest cost?
options: Two HA VPN gateways with four IPsec tunnels per gateway spread across two separate Google edge nodes — HA VPN provides 99.99% SLA through redundant IPsec tunnels over the internet; it does not offer the dedicated private bandwidth of Dedicated Interconnect connections at the same capacity
A Partner Interconnect with two 10 Gbps VLAN attachments through the same service provider
Cross-Cloud Interconnect with redundant 100 Gbps ports terminating at the colocation facility
Two 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections in different Edge Availability Domains at one metro
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect with two 10 Gbps links placed in different Edge Availability Domains at the same metropolitan area meets the 99.99% topology requirement. HA VPN runs over the public internet, is best-effort rather than dedicated, and is capped at roughly 3 Gbps per tunnel pair. Partner Interconnect routes through a partner's network, adding latency and provider markup. Cross-Cloud Interconnect connects GCP to other public clouds, not to a customer colocation.

questions.question: Twelve project VPCs need full-mesh reachability with each other and with on-premises sites attached via Dedicated Interconnect. The platform team wants to avoid managing dozens of peering relationships and prefers a managed transit topology. Which design fits best?
options: Build VPC Network Peering between every pair of project VPCs and let subnet routes propagate transitively — VPC peering does not support transitive routing; peered VPCs cannot reach on-premises resources or third-party networks through another peered VPC without Network Connectivity Center
Use Network Connectivity Center with one VPC as the hub and each project VPC plus the Interconnect attachment as spokes

Build full-mesh IPsec VPN tunnels between every pair of VPCs, then attach the on-premises Interconnect as a spoke in each VPC — full-mesh topology does not support transitive routing and does not scale for twelve projects sharing on-premises connectivity
Consolidate all projects into a single Shared VPC host project with twelve service projects sharing one subnet plan
questions.explanation: Network Connectivity Center (NCC) provides a managed hub-and-spoke topology in which VPC spokes receive full-mesh reachability through the hub, and hybrid attachments (Interconnect or HA VPN) become hybrid spokes on the same hub. VPC Peering is non-transitive, forcing an N×(N-1)/2 mesh. Inter-VPC VPN tunnels are operationally heavy. Shared VPC eliminates the separate VPCs entirely, which the question rules out by keeping per-project VPCs.

questions.question: The security team operates an existing Suricata-based intrusion detection platform and wants full packet payload visibility on selected backend instances behind an internal load balancer. VPC Flow Logs are already enabled. What should they add?
options: Increase VPC Flow Logs sampling to 1.0 and enable all metadata fields so payload inspection data appears in Cloud Logging — VPC Flow Logs capture connection metadata such as source and destination IP and port; they do not include packet payload content required for deep-packet inspection of internal traffic

Enable Firewall Insights on the target instances and export the resulting logs to a Pub/Sub topic — Firewall Insights reports on firewall rule usage and shadow rules, not packet payloads required for deep-packet inspection of internal traffic
Configure Packet Mirroring on the target instances with a collector internal LB fronting the Suricata appliances

Replace VPC Flow Logs with Cloud IDS in the VPC — Cloud IDS detects known threat signatures using Suricata-compatible rule sets but does not forward full packet mirrors to an existing external Suricata appliance fleet for custom rule evaluation
questions.explanation: Packet Mirroring clones full packet payloads (headers and body) from selected sources to a collector internal load balancer fronting custom IDS appliances such as Suricata. VPC Flow Logs only ever capture 5-tuple metadata, regardless of sampling rate or fields. Firewall Insights analyzes firewall rule usage, not packet contents. Cloud IDS is Google's managed IDS — useful, but it does not feed an existing Suricata platform.

questions.question: GCE VMs in a subnet have only internal IP addresses and need to call BigQuery and Cloud Storage at their standard public endpoints. No Cloud NAT is deployed and adding external IPs is not allowed. What is the minimum configuration to enable this?
options: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet so traffic to Google API endpoints uses Google's private network

Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in the region and enable internet egress so the VMs can reach Google API endpoints — Cloud NAT routes traffic through public NAT IPs to the internet rather than routing privately to Google APIs as Private Google Access does

Create a Private Service Connect endpoint for each Google API in the subnet and update client libraries to use the new endpoint URL — PSC also provides private access but requires endpoint provisioning per API and library changes, unlike Private Google Access which requires only a subnet flag
Set up VPC Network Peering between the workload VPC and Google's managed services VPC to reach the APIs privately
questions.explanation: Private Google Access is a subnet-level toggle that lets VMs with only internal IPs reach the public IPs of Google APIs over Google's private network — no NAT, no external IPs, no client changes. Cloud NAT also works but adds infrastructure and cost the question explicitly excludes. Private Service Connect creates private endpoints with different URLs, requiring client config changes. There is no VPC peering arrangement to Google's services VPC.

questions.question: A public-facing HTTPS service behind a global external Application Load Balancer is receiving a volumetric Layer 7 flood from a small set of source IP ranges, plus SQL-injection-style request patterns. The team needs to block the abusive IPs and the malicious request signatures at the edge without changing the backends. What should they configure?
options: A hierarchical firewall policy at the organization node denying the offending source ranges on TCP 443
A Cloud Armor security policy on the load balancer's backend service with IP deny rules and a preconfigured SQLi WAF rule
VPC firewall rules on the backend instances denying the source ranges, plus Packet Mirroring to a WAF appliance
A Cloud CDN negative-caching rule that drops requests matching the malicious URL patterns before they reach origin
questions.explanation: Cloud Armor attaches to the global external Application Load Balancer's backend service and enforces edge security policies: IP/CIDR allow-deny rules plus preconfigured WAF rules (e.g. the OWASP SQLi rule set) that inspect Layer 7 request content. Hierarchical and VPC firewall rules act at Layer 3/4 on instances, not on L7 request payloads at the edge, and the global ALB front end isn't filtered by instance firewall rules anyway. Cloud CDN caches responses and does not perform WAF inspection or IP-based access control for security.

questions.question: Two custom-mode VPCs, vpc-a (10.10.0.0/16) and vpc-b (10.20.0.0/16), are connected with VPC Network Peering. After peering is active, instances in vpc-a still cannot reach instances in vpc-b. Firewall rules on both sides already allow the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
options: VPC Network Peering does not exchange subnet routes by default, so custom route exchange or import/export settings must be enabled
Peered VPCs must reside in the same region, and these subnets are in different regions
The two VPCs have overlapping IP ranges, which silently disables the peering connection
Peering requires the same autonomous system number on both Cloud Routers before routes propagate
questions.explanation: VPC Network Peering automatically exchanges subnet (and subnet secondary) routes between the peered VPCs once the connection is ACTIVE — but if the peering was configured without exchanging subnet routes, or relies on custom (static/dynamic) routes that aren't being exported/imported, reachability fails even with permissive firewalls; verifying the route exchange/import-export configuration is the fix. Peering works across regions; the ranges 10.10.0.0/16 and 10.20.0.0/16 do not overlap; and peering does not use Cloud Router ASNs to propagate subnet routes.

questions.question: An on-premises network is connected to a GCP VPC over HA VPN with Cloud Router using BGP. The on-premises team adds new subnets frequently and wants GCP to learn them automatically, while GCP should advertise only its own VPC subnets — not a default route — to on-premises. How should the Cloud Router be configured?
options: Disable BGP and use static routes for every on-premises subnet, updating them whenever a new subnet appears
Set the Cloud Router to default (automatic) advertisement mode and add a custom advertised route for 0.0.0.0/0
Rely on BGP dynamic route learning for on-premises prefixes and leave the Cloud Router on default advertisement mode advertising VPC subnets
Switch the Cloud Router to custom advertisement mode advertising 0.0.0.0/0 so on-premises always has a path
questions.explanation: With BGP on Cloud Router, on-premises prefixes are learned dynamically as the on-prem router advertises them — no manual updates needed. Leaving Cloud Router in default advertisement mode automatically advertises the VPC's own subnets (and not a default route), exactly matching the requirement. Static routes defeat the goal of automatic learning; advertising 0.0.0.0/0 (a default route) is explicitly not wanted; custom mode advertising 0.0.0.0/0 likewise pushes a default route on-premises.

questions.question: A managed instance group of backend VMs sits behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. During rolling deployments, clients intermittently hit instances that are still booting and not yet ready to serve. The team wants the load balancer to stop sending new connections to an instance until the application port responds. What should they configure?
options: A higher session affinity setting on the backend service so connections stick to already-warm instances
Connection draining with a 300-second timeout on the forwarding rule to delay new traffic during deploys
A larger minimum number of instances in the managed instance group to absorb the booting period
A health check on the backend service that probes the application's port, so only healthy instances receive traffic
questions.explanation: A load balancer health check that probes the application's serving port marks instances UNHEALTHY until they respond, so the internal passthrough Network Load Balancer withholds new connections from instances that are still booting — directly solving the problem. Session affinity only pins existing client-to-backend mappings; connection draining gracefully finishes in-flight connections to removed backends, not gating new ones to booting instances; and a larger MIG size adds capacity but still routes traffic to not-yet-ready instances without a health check.
questions.domain: Managing, monitoring, and optimizing network operations

questions.question: A platform team is designing a new VPC for a large enterprise that already operates many on-premises networks. They want a single VPC where they explicitly define every subnet and its region, avoiding any automatically created subnets that could overlap with existing on-premises ranges. Which VPC type and approach should they choose?
options: An auto-mode VPC, then delete the unneeded automatically generated subnets after creation
A custom-mode VPC in which the team manually defines each subnet's CIDR and region
A legacy (non-subnet) network so the whole VPC uses one global IP range with no per-region subnets
An auto-mode VPC converted to custom mode, keeping the default 10.128.0.0/9 subnets for compatibility
questions.explanation: A custom-mode VPC creates no subnets automatically; the team defines each subnet's CIDR and region explicitly, which is the recommended approach for enterprises avoiding overlap with existing on-premises RFC1918 ranges. Auto-mode pre-creates a subnet in every region from the predictable 10.128.0.0/9 block, risking overlap, and cleanup is error-prone. Legacy networks are deprecated and lack regional subnets/modern features. Converting auto-to-custom while keeping the default subnets retains the very overlapping ranges they want to avoid.
questions.domain: Designing, planning, and prototyping a Google Cloud network

questions.question: VMs in a subnet have only internal IP addresses and must make outbound connections to third-party SaaS APIs on the public internet (not Google APIs). Adding external IPs to the VMs is prohibited by policy. What is the recommended managed way to provide this outbound internet access?
options: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet so the VMs can reach the third-party public endpoints privately
Configure Cloud NAT with a Cloud Router in the region to provide outbound-only NAT for the subnet
Create a Private Service Connect endpoint targeting the third-party API's published service
Assign a shared external IP to the subnet's default gateway so all VMs egress through it
questions.explanation: Cloud NAT, paired with a Cloud Router, gives instances with only internal IPs outbound-only access to the public internet (including arbitrary third-party SaaS endpoints) without assigning external IPs — the recommended managed pattern. Private Google Access only reaches Google's own API endpoints, not arbitrary third-party services. Private Service Connect connects to published producer services, not the general internet. There is no concept of assigning an external IP to a subnet's gateway in GCP.
